---
# The Department of Minor Returns

The first thing anyone brought back was a door.

This was awkward because the sign above the counter said SMALL OBJECTS ONLY, and because the woman carrying the door had come on the bus. She had persuaded the driver to let her stand with it in the space reserved for folded strollers, on the grounds that it folded in a sense. She demonstrated by opening and closing it on one remaining hinge. The driver, who was late and had spent fifteen years learning which arguments would make him later, let her on.

“Where did you find it?” I asked.

“It’s mine,” she said.

“Then you don’t need us.”

“I know whose it was before it was mine. That’s the trouble.”

The door was painted yellow on one side and unpainted on the other. A little brass hook, too high for a child to reach, protruded from the frame. At the bottom was a black crescent where, the woman explained, a dog named Albert had once scratched to be let in.

“Is Albert the party you wish to return it to?”

She looked at me for a long time. I was twenty-three and still thought a joke could make most kinds of paperwork less humiliating.

“No,” she said. “Albert would have wanted to keep it.”

Our office occupied the old municipal baths, behind the library and below a clock that had been wrong for so long people gave directions by the wrongness. If you were meeting someone at noon, you could say, “When the baths say twenty past four,” and nobody would ask what you meant. The city had intended to put a youth orchestra in the building, then a court for parking appeals, then a museum devoted to the canal. What finally moved in was a woman named Ada, six metal shelves, and a budget line that could not, without amending an ordinance, be spent on anything other than returning property.

Ada was my supervisor. When I asked her what counted as property, she said, “If somebody comes looking for it, don’t start by telling them it doesn’t count.”

She came out from the back room and looked at the door.

“Do you have the house?” she asked the woman.

“Not anymore. They knocked it down on Thursday.”

“Do you have a name?”

“My sister’s. But we haven’t spoken in eleven years.”

Ada handed her our standard form. The woman filled in her sister’s name, her own phone number, and, in the box marked CONDITION, the words *better than you’d expect*. Then she went home on the same bus, in the same space, with her hands free. I watched from the window as she moved aside to let a man maneuver a stroller past her. She made a little flourish with both arms, as though she had herself invented the room he needed.

We leaned the door against the wall and put a numbered tag on the brass hook.

For a while we took in ordinary things. A set of dentures in a raspberry jam jar. A trumpet whose case contained, instead of a mouthpiece, eleven hard-boiled eggs. A photograph of a woman cutting the ribbon at the opening of a laundromat that still existed, though the woman did not. When I phoned the laundromat, the owner said she was his aunt and he would come on Saturday. He came on Tuesday. He stood at the counter touching the picture with one finger, just below his aunt’s shoes.

“I was there,” he said. “They made me hold the other end of the ribbon. I was furious they wouldn’t let me have the scissors.”

He kept looking. I began to wonder if he expected to see himself at the edge.

“Do you want an envelope?” I asked.

“No. I live over the shop. I’ll walk her home.”

That was our first completed return. Ada rang the little bell on the counter. Then she told me not to do it again unless we were both in the room; she didn’t want me to have all the fun.

The door stayed through winter. Sometimes I used its unpainted side as a clipboard, until Ada pointed out that I had pressed an impression of a set of dentures into the wood. We sent a postcard to the sister at the last address the woman knew. It came back marked NO SUCH NUMBER. I looked up the street and found that the numbers skipped from 16 to 20. Number 18 had disappeared into a driveway, and the house at 20 had a basketball hoop over its garage. You could see it on the city’s map. For months afterward, whenever I mailed something important, I caught myself picturing that hoop.

In February, a man brought in a red mitten. He had found it on the river path and attached it to a fence, where it remained for nine days. On the tenth day it rained. He took the mitten home and dried it over a radiator.

“Is there anything distinctive about it?” I asked, opening the ledger.

“It’s very small.”

“Anything else?”

“I used to buy them like this.”

He made a shape with his hands, indicating a child of intermediate size who might have been five or six. Then he put his hands in his pockets.

We did not find the owner of the mitten. In April he brought in a blue cap. In June, a tiny green shoe. He always stayed until I had written a description, and I began to understand that part of what mattered to him was watching the details go down. For the shoe, I wrote *one green canvas shoe, left, size seven, white rubber toe, considerably worn*. He asked me to change *considerably* to *a little*. I did. It made no difference to the prospects of a return, and by then I had learned to distinguish the rules Ada cared about from the ones I had invented because I liked the sound of my pen stopping.

My mother called every Sunday, usually while the kettle was on. She and my father had moved to a town where the grocery store sold frozen bait in the same freezer as the ice cream, which was her preferred example of how well they had adjusted. At some point in every call, she gave me a chance to report that I was leaving the baths for a better job.

“Anything on the horizon?” she would say.

There were a number of jobs I meant to apply for. I kept their descriptions in a folder on my desktop, sometimes after the closing dates, out of a reluctance I would have been hard put to explain. I liked coming in early and listening to Ada fill the kettle in the old dressing room. I liked how the pipes knocked when the heating came on. I also wanted a salary that would let me buy a winter coat without standing in the shop calculating my remaining days in the month. Mostly I wanted my mother to stop asking so I could tell her, without being asked, what I did all day.

One morning a boy of about twelve came in with nothing in his hands.

“I lost my brother’s laugh,” he said.

Ada had gone to the dentist. I was eating toast over the ledger, which she would not have allowed.

“When did you last have it?” I asked.

The boy pulled up a chair. His brother wasn’t dead, it turned out. He had moved two streets away with their father. They still saw one another, but the brother had developed a new laugh, an economical breath through his nose with which he acknowledged things on his phone. The old laugh was the one that came out when he tried not to laugh during dinner. It began, the boy said, with a sound like a duck being stepped on.

I didn’t open the ledger. It was clear to me that we couldn’t return a laugh, and pretty clear that the boy knew it, too.

“Can you do it?” I asked.

“No.”

He thought for a moment. Then he lowered his head and tried. The result was a rude little quack. From what he’d told me about the laugh, I imagined it wasn’t very close. But it was an excellent sound to hear in a tiled building at nine in the morning. I laughed, and so did he, though not in the way he had come in hoping to hear.

After he left, I tipped the toast crumbs out of the ledger into my palm. I did not make an entry. I’ve sometimes wished I had, because I can remember the brother’s laugh as described but can no longer remember the boy’s.

The letter telling us we were to close arrived in August, tucked into a shipment of stationery meant to last until the next financial year. Ada read it twice, worked the staple free with her thumbnail, and posted the second page on the front door. It explained that unclaimed objects would be transferred to central storage, pending appropriate disposal. The document had been written by someone who knew that *pending* was a good word to put before something nobody wanted to picture.

“How much time do we have?” I asked.

“Six weeks.”

“What are we going to do?”

“What we did yesterday. More urgently, I suppose.”

We moved the shelves into what had been the shallow end. With the objects laid out in daylight, they looked less like exhibits than the contents of an apartment whose tenant had stepped out in a great hurry. We found the owner of the trumpet; he said the eggs weren’t his. We found an engineer who could identify her own umbrella by the replacement screw in its handle, and an elderly woman who brought in the matching earring to one we’d held for a year. The two earrings lay together on the counter like shy cousins. Watching her put them on, I understood why she’d bothered. They made two very small flashes every time she turned her head.

I called the woman who had brought us the door. I must have sounded apologetic, because she interrupted to say it was all right, she knew her sister’s address.

“Since when?” I asked.

“Since before I brought it in.”

She told me where it was, in a town forty minutes away by train. She had written the old address on our form because it was the last one her sister had given her. The new one she knew from a nephew’s wedding invitation somebody had left face-up on a kitchen table.

“I was hoping you’d find her some other way,” she said.

I looked down the room at the door. In summer the yellow was almost too bright to look at, but a little rectangle below the handle, where an old sticker had been peeled away, was brighter still.

“Would you like the door back?” I asked.

“I want to know if she wants it.”

I said I could write and ask. The woman didn’t speak for a while. Then she asked whether I could send her whatever I wrote, so she could see it before it went out.

It took three drafts. In the first, I called the door an *item of possible sentimental significance*, which Ada crossed out so hard she tore the paper. In the second, I got halfway through explaining the circumstances under which we had obtained the door before noticing that I’d made it sound as though we had confiscated it. The one we sent said there was a yellow door at the municipal baths, that it had come from her old house, and that her sister had brought it to us. We would be open until the end of September. Here was our number.

The sister phoned the next day. Had it still got the brass hook? I said yes.

“Our mother put that up,” she said. “To stop the dog getting in. It didn’t stop him. He could get through if it was open even an inch. He’d lie down and push his nose into it.”

“Albert,” I said.

“No, before Albert. This was a much worse dog.”

She wanted to come on Friday. I asked if she wanted her sister to be there. She said she’d call her herself.

That Friday I wore a shirt without a missing button. This turned out to be the full extent of my involvement. The sisters met outside, where I couldn’t hear them. One held up a packet of biscuits for the other to see. After a while they came in together and stood at an angle to the door, as though waiting for someone on the other side to answer.

The sister who’d brought the door asked if we remembered what she’d written about its condition. I found the form. She read it aloud and they both laughed, although the other sister said, “Well, you would say that. You never could see a thing wrong with this color.”

“I picked that color,” the first sister said.

“I know.”

They stood looking at it a little longer. Neither of them had anywhere to put it. One lived in a narrow upstairs flat, the other in a house with doors that fit. We took it out to the pavement anyway, to see whether the fresh air would give anyone an idea. There it looked enormous.

In the end they took the brass hook. I fetched a screwdriver and held the frame while one sister worked the screws loose. She gave the hook to the other to hold, then went after the screws, which had rolled apart on the pavement. They left with the biscuits and the hardware in the same coat pocket. I propped the door against the counter one last time and rang the bell. Ada had to come out of the back room to ask what I thought I was doing.

“The hook,” I said.

“Oh,” she said. “Of course.”

On our final afternoon the man who had brought us the red mitten came in. I thought he might be looking for something new to hand over, but he wanted to know what would happen to the shoe. I explained about central storage. Then I asked if he wanted it. He looked startled, as if I had offered him one of my own.

“I wouldn’t know what to do with it,” he said.

We stood there awhile. In the end he went home without it. I was glad he’d come, though I still don’t know what he wanted me to tell him. Perhaps he’d hoped the shoe was already gone. I could have told him that, but the empty shelves behind me made it hard to say anything that wasn’t true.

The baths stood empty for seven years. When they reopened, as a branch library and community kitchen, I came down for the opening. The clock had been repaired. I arrived twenty minutes late, having gotten so used to subtracting them that I’d done it one last time.

Outside the kitchen was a long yellow bench. I went around behind it and put my hand under the seat. There, where you wouldn’t notice it unless you ran your fingers along the grain, was the little black crescent. I asked a volunteer where they’d gotten the wood. She said it had been lying in the building when they started work. There’d been just enough sound timber for a seat. They’d had to buy the legs.

I sat down. Through the open kitchen window I could hear someone hunting for scissors. A woman beside me was easing an orange out of a string bag. When she had peeled it, she offered me half, and I took it. It was colder than I’d expected, as though she had carried it all the way from her refrigerator just in time to share it with a stranger. I held the peel for her while she ate. Then we went inside to see if anyone had found the scissors.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A quietly comic, emotionally layered short story built around a municipal lost-property office and the people who bring things there.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant and gently funny, with humor that eases embarrassment rather than mocking it. Its pathos comes from the gap between what can be returned and what people actually miss: a door becomes a route back toward an estranged sister, while a boy’s attempt to recover his brother’s old laugh can only produce a new shared one. The narrator is attentive to small gestures and material details—the brass hook, a mitten described as “a little” worn, half an orange offered to a stranger—and remains modest about what those gestures can accomplish. The story invites the reader to treat care as a form of attention, even when repair is partial and the people doing the caring cannot make everything right.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story centers lost objects as carriers of memory, grief, and unfinished relationships. It gives particular weight to ordinary acts of stewardship: recording details accurately, making room for someone else, and asking whether a thing—or its history—should go home. Its mood is elegiac but not bleak; the office closes, objects remain unresolved, and yet the story ends with a small, unceremonious act of sharing.

## Evidence line
> I liked how the pipes knocked when the heating came on.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the recurring attention to overlooked objects, restrained humor, and partial rather than miraculous reconciliations makes this a distinctive, coherent sample of a humane and quietly elegiac narrative voice.
